claims.claim: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made.
The relevant opportunity cost is only the single most valuable forgone alternative, not the combined value of every option passed up.

Explicit costs are out-of-pocket payments (wages, rent), while implicit costs are the opportunity cost of resources the decision-maker already owns; economic profit subtracts both, accounting profit only the explicit costs.
Opportunity cost applies to time and other resources, not only money; the true cost of a choice includes forgone alternatives beyond direct monetary expenditure.

The production possibilities frontier shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology; the slope between two points is the opportunity cost of the additional production.

The law of increasing opportunity cost holds that as production of a good increases, the marginal opportunity cost of producing more of it rises; this bows the PPF outward because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods.
The concept grew out of the late-19th-century marginalist tradition and the term is commonly credited to the Austrian economist Friedrich von Wieser (1851-1925).
A sunk cost is an already-incurred, unrecoverable expense and is not an opportunity cost; rational forward-looking decisions ignore sunk costs.

positions: Commonly credited to Friedrich von Wieser, who coined the German term and developed the idea within Austrian/marginalist value theory
The underlying trade-off logic is older and diffuse across the marginalist revolution (Menger, Jevons, Walras); attribution to any single figure is an oversimplification
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Attribute the concept to the marginalist tradition and name Wieser modestly as the economist commonly credited with the term, not as sole inventor of the idea.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 2.1: How Individuals Make Choices Based on Their Budget Constraint
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Supports that 'opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative' and that people must give up something to obtain what they desire; the Alphonso budget-constraint example shows opportunity cost is measured in the forgone alternative (four bus tickets for one burger) rather than only the dollar price; the airport-security example shows opportunity cost of travelers' time is a real cost beyond monetary expenditure. Facts synthesized in original prose; no extended passages reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 2.2: The Production Possibilities Frontier and Social Choices
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Supports the definition of the production possibilities frontier as the set of production combinations available given resources and technology; the statement that the slope of the PPF between two points is the opportunity cost of the additional production; the law of increasing opportunity cost (as production of a good increases, its marginal opportunity cost rises); and the bowed-outward shape arising because resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods. Uses the healthcare-vs-education illustration. No passages reproduced beyond short definitional phrases.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 7.1: Explicit and Implicit Costs, and Accounting and Economic Profit
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Supports: explicit costs are out-of-pocket payments (wages, rent); implicit costs represent the opportunity cost of using resources the firm already owns; accounting profit is total revenue minus explicit costs; economic profit is total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs. Used for the explicit/implicit distinction and the sunk-cost contrast (chapter treats forward-looking cost). No passages reproduced beyond short definitional phrases.
